grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: Who created the God of the Bible? The question and the method
resposta: This theme's question: does the God described in the Bible look more like a loving divine being, or like the mindset of the people who wrote about him, in a specific time and place? The same book says “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;” (Exodus 20:5) and also “He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.” (1 John 4:8). To understand this tension we follow what historical research, archaeology and psychology show, step by step, with the verse and the source for each claim.
aprofundar:
Two honest corrections first. One: the Bible was not written by a single person. Scholarship points to many authors, editors and schools over roughly a thousand years. Two: controlling people was one function of these texts, but not the only one. They also gave a small people an identity, explained wars and disasters, and held the group together in exile. Science neither proves nor disproves God's existence. What it can examine is the text: who wrote it, when and why.

camada3: To contemplate: asking where an idea came from is not attacking those who love it. It is taking it seriously.

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: Who wrote the Bible: many hands, many centuries
resposta: Tradition says Moses wrote the first five books, but the text itself narrates his death (Deut 34). Since the 19th century, scholars have identified distinct sources with their own style, names for God and interests. The classic labels are J (Yahwist), E (Elohist), D (Deuteronomist) and P (Priestly), in the documentary hypothesis popularized by Richard Friedman's 'Who Wrote the Bible?' (1987). Many today prefer supplementary models, where a base text receives layers over time. A landmark is “And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.” (2 Kings 22:8): King Josiah (c. 622 BC) 'finds' a law book, which most scholars link to the core of Deuteronomy, written or revised to support his religious and political reform.
aprofundar:
The P layer and much of the final editing come from the Babylonian exile and after (6th–5th centuries BC). Genesis 1 is a priestly text, and even there a plural appears: “And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.” (Genesis 1:26). So the God of the Bible was described by priests, court scribes, prophets and editors, each with concerns of their own: the temple, the king, loyalty to the one God, the survival of the people. Sources: documentary hypothesis — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_hypothesis ; Friedman — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who_Wrote_the_Bible%3F

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): 2 Kings 22:8 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2+Kings+22%3A8&version=KJV | Genesis 1:26 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+1%3A26&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: if many people wrote it, each left some of their fear, hope and politics in the text.

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: Where Yahweh came from: a storm god from the south
resposta: The name of God most used in the Hebrew Bible is YHWH (Yahweh). The oldest texts say he came from the south, from Seir, Edom and Teman, not from Israel: “And he said, The LORD came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them; he shined forth from mount Paran, and he came with ten thousands of saints: from his right hand went a fiery law for them.” (Deuteronomy 33:2) And also “LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, and the heavens dropped, the clouds also dropped water.” (Judges 5:4) Egyptian inscriptions from the 14th–13th centuries BC mention 'the Shasu of YHW', nomads of that region. So many scholars, like Thomas Römer in 'The Invention of God' (Harvard, 2015), think Yahweh began as a storm and war god of southern groups (Midianites or Kenites) and was only later adopted in Israel.
aprofundar:
A telling detail: a storm and war god is described with thunder, fire, earthquake and victory in battle, exactly the imagery of many ancient texts about Yahweh (Judg 5:4–5; Ps 18; Hab 3:3). It is a well-grounded hypothesis, not a closed fact, and details are still debated. Sources: Yahweh — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahweh ; Kenite hypothesis — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenite_hypothesis ; Römer — https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674504974

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Deuteronomy 33:2 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Deuteronomy+33%3A2&version=KJV | Judges 5:4 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Judges+5%3A4&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: a god born as a tribe's warrior carries that tribe's way of thinking.

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: El, Asherah and 'God's wife': the Canaanite pantheon
resposta: In the Ugaritic texts (c. 1300 BC, in today's Syria), the high god is El, his consort is Asherah, and they have 70 sons, the 'sons of El', each linked to a people. The Bible keeps echoes of this. The KJV has “When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel.” (Deuteronomy 32:8), but the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint read 'according to the number of the sons of God', which recalls El's 70 sons, one per nation. And the Psalm says: “God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.” (Psalms 82:1)
aprofundar:
Archaeology confirms a goddess worshipped alongside Yahweh. At Kuntillet Ajrud (c. 800 BC), jars carry the blessing 'by Yahweh of Samaria and his Asherah'. The Bible shows people baking cakes for the 'queen of heaven': “The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead their dough, to make cakes to the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto other gods, that they may provoke me to anger.” (Jeremiah 7:18) And in Josiah's reform, “And the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and the priests of the second order, and the keepers of the door, to bring forth out of the temple of the LORD all the vessels that were made for Baal, and for the grove, and for all the host of heaven: and he burned them without Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron, and carried the ashes of them unto Bethel.” (2 Kings 23:4) For centuries, many Israelites worshipped Yahweh along with other deities, and 'Yahweh alone' won later. Mark S. Smith, in 'The Early History of God', shows Yahweh absorbing El's titles and gradually the other gods' roles. Sources: Kuntillet Ajrud — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuntillet_Ajrud ; Asherah — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asherah ; Smith — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Early_History_of_God

camada3: To contemplate: ideas about God changed over time. A changing image follows whoever draws it.

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: From many gods to one: monotheism is born in exile
resposta: The oldest texts don't deny that other gods exist. They demand that Israel serve Yahweh alone. That is monolatry: “For thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God:” (Exodus 34:14) The Bible names neighboring gods plainly: “Because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon, and have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in mine eyes, and to keep my statutes and my judgments, as did David his father.” (1 Kings 11:33) Full monotheism, the idea that only one God exists, emerges strongly in Second Isaiah, written during the Babylonian exile (c. 540 BC): “I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me:” (Isaiah 45:5)
aprofundar:
Why in exile? Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed in 586 BC. A defeated people had two options: accept that Babylon's gods were stronger, or say Yahweh himself had used Babylon to punish Israel. The scribes chose the second. So Yahweh became responsible for everything, even evil: “I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things.” (Isaiah 45:7) This is the root of 'punishment for sins': defeat becomes the people's guilt rather than God's weakness. Sources: monolatry — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monolatry ; exile — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babylonian_captivity

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Exodus 34:14 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus+34%3A14&version=KJV | Isaiah 45:5 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Isaiah+45%3A5&version=KJV | Isaiah 45:7 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Isaiah+45%3A7&version=KJV | 1 Kings 11:33 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Kings+11%3A33&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: when a people suffers it looks for an explanation. Guilt tends to be the one that binds most.

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: The warrior God and the kings of the ancient Near East
resposta: How Yahweh acts in war was the standard of the age. On the Mesha Stele (c. 840 BC, Louvre), the king of Moab says his god Chemosh ordered him to attack Nebo, and that he killed its 7,000 inhabitants, men, women and girls, because he had 'devoted them to destruction' (the same idea as the biblical 'herem'). The Bible itself tells of the war against this king and says that when he sacrificed his son, “Then he took his eldest son that should have reigned in his stead, and offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall. And there was great indignation against Israel: and they departed from him, and returned to their own land.” (2 Kings 3:27)
aprofundar:
Deuteronomy also copies the form of Assyrian vassal treaties. Esarhaddon's succession treaty (672 BC) required reporting even one's own relative who conspired against the king, and lists curses such as eating the flesh of one's own children. Compare “If thy brother, the son of thy mother, or thy son, or thy daughter, or the wife of thy bosom, or thy friend, which is as thine own soul, entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, which thou hast not known, thou, nor thy fathers;” (Deuteronomy 13:6) and “And thou shalt eat the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters, which the LORD thy God hath given thee, in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee:” (Deuteronomy 28:53) Many scholars (Levinson, Steymans, Römer) see Judahite scribes swapping the Assyrian emperor for Yahweh as the 'great king' owed total loyalty. Sources: Mesha Stele — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesha_Stele ; herem — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herem_(war_or_property) ; Esarhaddon — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esarhaddon

camada3: To contemplate: if the God of the text acts like the kings of the age, it is fair to ask who modeled whom.

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
resposta:
Here are the texts as they are, in full. Next to each, how the same order would be judged today under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998).

1) Numbers 31, after the war against Midian, Moses says: “Now therefore kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman that hath known man by lying with him.” (Numbers 31:17) “But all the women children, that have not known a man by lying with him, keep alive for yourselves.” (Numbers 31:18) Today: genocide (art. 6), killing prisoners and children (art. 8) and sexual slavery (arts. 7.1.g and 8.2.b.xxii).

2) “But of the cities of these people, which the LORD thy God doth give thee for an inheritance, thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth:” (Deuteronomy 20:16) “But thou shalt utterly destroy them; namely, the Hittites, and the Amorites, the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites; as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee:” (Deuteronomy 20:17) Today: genocide (art. 6) and an order of 'no survivors', a war crime (art. 8.2.b.xii).

3) “Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.” (1 Samuel 15:3) Today: genocide (art. 6) and intentional attack on civilians (art. 8.2.b.i).

4) At Jericho: “And they utterly destroyed all that was in the city, both man and woman, young and old, and ox, and sheep, and ass, with the edge of the sword.” (Joshua 6:21) Today: genocide and a crime against humanity (arts. 6 and 7).

5) “And it came to pass, that at midnight the LORD smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sat on his throne unto the firstborn of the captive that was in the dungeon; and all the firstborn of cattle.” (Exodus 12:29) Today: collective punishment of children for a ruler's decision, banned by Geneva Convention IV (art. 33).

6) The flood: “And every living substance was destroyed which was upon the face of the ground, both man, and cattle, and the creeping things, and the fowl of the heaven; and they were destroyed from the earth: and Noah only remained alive, and they that were with him in the ark.” (Genesis 7:23) Today: extermination (art. 7.1.b).
aprofundar:
Behaviour traits these texts describe, without diagnosis: collective punishment (the innocent pay for the group), dehumanization of the other people (all become 'enemies' to destroy) and sparing only virgins treated as spoils. Diagnosing a literary character is neither possible nor honest. What can be said is: a human giving these orders today would stand trial for war crimes.

Two balancing facts: (1) archaeology indicates many of these conquests did not happen as told. Jericho, for example, was practically uninhabited at the time attributed to Joshua (Kathleen Kenyon, 1950s; Finkelstein, 'The Bible Unearthed'). These are identity narratives written centuries later, not war reports. (2) The pattern matches the Mesha Stele: this is how peoples of that age imagined a victorious god. Sources: Rome Statute — https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/RS-Eng.pdf ; Geneva IV art. 33 — https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/gciv-1949/article-33 ; Jericho — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jericho

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: The hardest verses (2): collective punishment and control by fear
resposta:
1) Against anyone, even family, who calls to another god: “If thy brother, the son of thy mother, or thy son, or thy daughter, or the wife of thy bosom, or thy friend, which is as thine own soul, entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, which thou hast not known, thou, nor thy fathers;” (Deuteronomy 13:6) “But thou shalt surely kill him; thine hand shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterwards the hand of all the people.” (Deuteronomy 13:9) “And thou shalt stone him with stones, that he die; because he hath sought to thrust thee away from the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage.” (Deuteronomy 13:10) Today: execution for belief, which violates the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (arts. 6 and 18).

2) In a vision, God sends six men through Jerusalem: “And to the others he said in mine hearing, Go ye after him through the city, and smite: let not your eye spare, neither have ye pity:” (Ezekiel 9:5) “Slay utterly old and young, both maids, and little children, and women: but come not near any man upon whom is the mark; and begin at my sanctuary. Then they began at the ancient men which were before the house.” (Ezekiel 9:6) Today: mass murder of civilians, a crime against humanity (art. 7.1.a).

3) Threat of extreme famine: “And ye shall eat the flesh of your sons, and the flesh of your daughters shall ye eat.” (Leviticus 26:29) Today, starving civilians as a weapon is a war crime (art. 8.2.b.xxv).

4) Elisha curses the boys in the name of the Lord: “And he went up from thence unto Bethel: and as he was going up by the way, there came forth little children out of the city, and mocked him, and said unto him, Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head.” (2 Kings 2:23) “And he turned back, and looked on them, and cursed them in the name of the LORD. And there came forth two she bears out of the wood, and tare forty and two children of them.” (2 Kings 2:24) Today: disproportionate killing of minors over a verbal insult.

5) Against Samaria: “Samaria shall become desolate; for she hath rebelled against her God: they shall fall by the sword: their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up.” (Hosea 13:16) Today: a war crime against children and pregnant women (art. 8).

6) After the golden calf: “And he said unto them, Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Put every man his sword by his side, and go in and out from gate to gate throughout the camp, and slay every man his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbour.” (Exodus 32:27) “And the children of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men.” (Exodus 32:28) Today: collective execution on religious grounds.

7) A man gathering sticks on the sabbath: “And the LORD said unto Moses, The man shall be surely put to death: all the congregation shall stone him with stones without the camp.” (Numbers 15:35) “And all the congregation brought him without the camp, and stoned him with stones, and he died; as the LORD commanded Moses.” (Numbers 15:36) Today: death penalty for working on a holy day, against the right to life (ICCPR art. 6).
aprofundar:
Behaviour traits described, without diagnosis: demand for exclusive loyalty (the 'jealous' one of Ex 34:14), surveillance and denunciation inside the family, collective punishment, threat as a means of obedience and disproportionate punishment. In the psychology of relationships this cluster (isolate, watch, threaten, punish whoever leaves) has a name: coercive control, described by sociologist Evan Stark (2007). It is not a diagnosis of God. It describes the kind of relationship these texts build between the people and authority, the same one Assyrian treaties built between vassal and emperor. Sources: Rome Statute — https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/RS-Eng.pdf ; ICCPR — https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights ; coercive control — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coercive_control

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: A God in the image of those who describe him: what psychology says
resposta: You cannot diagnose a character in a book; doing so would be as unscientific as calling him perfect. But patterns can be compared. The traits the texts give Yahweh match the ideals of an ancient Near Eastern warrior king: jealousy and a demand for exclusive loyalty (“Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;” (Exodus 20:5)), total destruction of the enemy (“And when the LORD thy God shall deliver them before thee; thou shalt smite them, and utterly destroy them; thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor shew mercy unto them:” (Deuteronomy 7:2)), collective punishment and reward for the obedient. Modern psychology studies these patterns in people and groups: dehumanization of the out-group (Nick Haslam, 2006), moral disengagement, which is justifying violence by a 'higher' cause (Albert Bandura), and collective punishment.
aprofundar:
And there is direct experimental data: in 2009 Nicholas Epley and colleagues (PNAS) showed that when religious people estimate what God thinks about controversial issues, the answer tracks their own opinion more than the opinion they attribute to others. When their own view shifted, their 'God' shifted with it. A modern hint of something ancient: each generation tends to describe God with its own mind. This fits your intuition, with one correction: not one person, but many generations of scribes, each putting the values and fears of their time into the text. Sources: Epley et al. 2009 — https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0908374106 ; moral disengagement — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_disengagement ; dehumanization — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehumanization

camada3: To contemplate: when someone says 'God wants this', it is worth gently asking: is it God, or me speaking through him?

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: From Sheol to hell: how eternal punishment was built
resposta: For almost the entire Old Testament there is no hell of torment. The dead go to Sheol, a dark, silent place for everyone, good and bad: “For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.” (Ecclesiastes 9:5) “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.” (Ecclesiastes 9:10) And the psalmist asks: “For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?” (Psalms 6:5) The first clear mention of different fates after death only appears in Daniel, written around 165 BC: “And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.” (Daniel 12:2)
aprofundar:
Between the exile and the time of Jesus, Judaism came into contact with Persian Zoroastrianism (final judgment, resurrection, cosmic battle of good and evil) and with Greek culture (immortal soul, Hades and Tartarus). The idea of punishment grew in that mix. The gospels have “Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:” (Matthew 25:41) “And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.” (Matthew 25:46) and “Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.” (Mark 9:48) 'Gehenna' was the valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem, remembered for ancient sacrifices. In Revelation: “And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.” (Revelation 14:11) Bart Ehrman, in 'Heaven and Hell' (2020), traces this evolution step by step. Eternal hell did not 'come from heaven' ready-made: it was built over some 400 years, and it is also the strongest fear tool ever used to obtain obedience. Sources: Sheol — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheol ; Gehenna — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gehenna ; Ehrman — https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Heaven-and-Hell/Bart-D-Ehrman/9781501136757

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: Gods who watch and punish: religion and social control
resposta: Your intuition that religion served to control has a scientific basis, but the story is fuller. Psychologist Ara Norenzayan, in 'Big Gods' (Princeton, 2013), proposes that all-seeing, punishing gods helped large societies cooperate among strangers: people who feel watched cheat less. A study across 8 societies (Purzycki et al., Nature, 2016) found more generosity toward distant co-religionists among those who believed in a moralizing, punishing god. In the Bible the formula is explicit: obedience brings blessing, and disobedience brings “I also will do this unto you; I will even appoint over you terror, consumption, and the burning ague, that shall consume the eyes, and cause sorrow of heart: and ye shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall eat it.” (Leviticus 26:16) and “But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:” (Deuteronomy 28:15)
aprofundar:
Scientific honesty: in 2019 a famous Nature study (Whitehouse et al.) claimed societies became complex before moralizing gods appeared. It was criticized for treating missing data as 'absence' (Beheim et al., Nature, 2021) and was retracted. The debate remains open. What is known: belief in a watching, punishing god increases cooperation and obedience within the group, and rulers can use that. But religion also gave identity, comfort in grief, an explanation for disasters and unity in exile. Control was an important function, not the only one. Sources: Norenzayan — https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691169743/big-gods ; Purzycki 2016 — https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16980 ; Whitehouse 2019 (retracted) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1043-4 ; Beheim 2021 — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03655-4

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Leviticus 26:16 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Leviticus+26%3A16&version=KJV | Deuteronomy 28:15 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Deuteronomy+28%3A15&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: feeling watched changes behaviour. It's worth knowing who holds the camera.

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: 'God is love' vs the texts: contradictions that invite questions
resposta: The Bible also says “He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.” (1 John 4:8), “The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.” (Psalms 145:9), “Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.” (Luke 6:36) and “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Micah 6:8) And it contradicts itself on inherited guilt. Exodus says “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;” (Exodus 20:5), but Ezekiel answers “The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.” (Ezekiel 18:20) These voices don't fit the massacre orders in the previous lessons. That is what you'd expect from a book written by many people, in different eras, with different ideas about God.
aprofundar:
How believers handle this, to be fair: in the 2nd century Marcion concluded the Old Testament God was a different god, and was declared a heretic. Origen read the massacres as allegories of inner struggle. Today apologists like Paul Copan ('Is God a Moral Monster?', 2011) say the texts use typical ancient war hyperbole, and theologians speak of 'progressive revelation'. Notice that all these answers admit that, read literally, the texts don't match a perfectly loving God. The simplest explanation, accepted by much academic research, is that they reflect the people and eras that wrote them. Sources: Marcion — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcionism ; Copan — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Copan ; problem of evil — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problem_of_evil

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): 1 John 4:8 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+John+4%3A8&version=KJV | Psalms 145:9 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalms+145%3A9&version=KJV | Luke 6:36 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+6%3A36&version=KJV | Micah 6:8 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Micah+6%3A8&version=KJV | Ezekiel 18:20 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ezekiel+18%3A20&version=KJV | Exodus 20:5 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus+20%3A5&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: you don't have to choose between swallowing everything and throwing it all away. You can keep 'be merciful' and leave the rest as the history of an age.

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: How a repeated idea becomes 'truth': the illusory truth effect
resposta: In 1977 Lynn Hasher and colleagues showed that statements heard several times seem truer than new ones, even when false. This is the illusory truth effect. In 2015 Lisa Fazio and colleagues showed it works even when people know the right answer: repetition creates familiarity, and the brain mistakes familiarity for truth. Add three reinforcers: hearing it from childhood from people we love; seeing adults make costly sacrifices for the faith (anthropologist Joseph Henrich calls these CREDs, 2009); and fear of questioning, when doubt is treated as sin and leaving can cost your family (compare “If thy brother, the son of thy mother, or thy son, or thy daughter, or the wife of thy bosom, or thy friend, which is as thine own soul, entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, which thou hast not known, thou, nor thy fathers;” (Deuteronomy 13:6)).
aprofundar:
This explains why intelligent, good people believe sincerely. They weren't foolish: they received a story repeated for generations, in an environment that rewarded accepting and punished doubting. A fair point: the effect applies to all of us, to any idea, including our own. The antidote is the same for any belief: go to the source, compare versions, ask 'how would I know if this were false?'. Sources: illusory truth effect — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusory_truth_effect ; Fazio et al. 2015 — https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000098 ; Henrich 2009 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2009.03.005

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Deuteronomy 13:6 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Deuteronomy+13%3A6&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: what idea have you never questioned just because you always heard it? Pick one and check the source, without fear.

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: What is true and what is not: who created the God of the Bible (table)
resposta: Scientific sum: 26 claims checked, one per row, with verse and source. Result: ✅ 16 match reality, ❌ 8 don't and ❔ 2 are not verifiable. Matching: many authors over centuries, Yahweh's southern origin, Asherah worship, monotheism born in exile, parallels with Mesha and the Assyrian treaties, what the massacre verses actually say, and the illusory truth effect. Not matching: a single author, one person inventing God to control, Jericho and the flood as narrated, a hell that always existed and a consistent text on inherited guilt. God's existence itself science neither proves nor refutes. Full table as cards: open conteudo/tabela-quem-criou-deus.html?lang=en or see below.
aprofundar:
Format: Claim (verse) · Verdict · Evidence — source. 'Matches reality' on massacre rows means: the text says exactly that.

1. The Bible was written by one person (Moses) or dictated ready-made from heaven (Deuteronomy 34:5)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   The text narrates Moses' death (Deut 34) and shows sources in different styles written over centuries. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_hypothesis

2. The texts were written and edited by many people over about a thousand years (2 Kings 22:8)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Academic consensus: J, E, D, P sources/layers and editing in and after the exile. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplementary_hypothesis

3. The 'book of the law' found by Josiah served a religious and political reform (2 Kings 22:8)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Most scholars link this book to the core of Deuteronomy (7th century BC). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josiah

4. Yahweh was described as a storm and war god coming from the south (Seir, Edom) (Judges 5:4; Deuteronomy 33:2)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Ancient biblical texts and Egyptian inscriptions about the 'Shasu of YHW' point to this origin (widely held hypothesis). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahweh

5. Israelites worshipped a goddess (Asherah, 'queen of heaven') along with Yahweh (Jeremiah 7:18; 2 Kings 23:4)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions (c. 800 BC): 'Yahweh of Samaria and his Asherah'. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuntillet_Ajrud

6. Ancient texts speak of a council of gods (Psalms 82:1; Deuteronomy 32:8)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Ps 82 and Deut 32:8 in the Dead Sea Scrolls ('sons of God') echo El's pantheon at Ugarit. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sons_of_God

7. Full monotheism gained strength in the Babylonian exile (Isaiah 45:5; Exodus 34:14)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Older texts demand loyalty to one god among others (monolatry); Isa 40–55 (c. 540 BC) denies other gods. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monolatry

8. Neighboring peoples had war gods who ordered cities exterminated (2 Kings 3:27)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Mesha Stele (c. 840 BC): Chemosh orders the attack on Nebo; 7,000 are 'devoted to destruction'. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesha_Stele

9. Deuteronomy uses the model of Assyrian loyalty treaties (Deuteronomy 13:6; Deuteronomy 28:53)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Parallels with Esarhaddon's treaty (672 BC): report relatives, curses of famine and cannibalism. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esarhaddon

10. The text orders killing boys and women and sparing virgins 'for yourselves' (Numbers 31:17; Numbers 31:18)
   ✅ Matches reality
   It is written so. Today: genocide and sexual slavery (Rome Statute, arts. 6, 7 and 8). — https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/RS-Eng.pdf

11. The text attributes to God orders to leave no survivors, including children (Deuteronomy 20:16; 1 Samuel 15:3)
   ✅ Matches reality
   It is written so. Today: genocide and a war crime (arts. 6 and 8.2.b.xii). — https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/RS-Eng.pdf

12. The conquest of Jericho happened as narrated (Joshua 6:21)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Jericho was practically uninhabited at the time attributed to Joshua (Kenyon; Finkelstein). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jericho

13. A worldwide flood killed all land life outside the ark (Genesis 7:23)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   There is no global geological layer from a recent flood; see the theme 'The math of the flood'. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood_geology

14. All the firstborn of Egypt died in one night (Exodus 12:29)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   There is no Egyptian record or archaeological evidence of the Exodus as narrated. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exodus

15. The text orders killing even a relative who invites you to worship another god (Deuteronomy 13:6; Deuteronomy 13:10)
   ✅ Matches reality
   It is written so. Today it would violate the right to life and freedom of religion (ICCPR, arts. 6 and 18). — https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights

16. The Bible always taught a hell of eternal torment (Ecclesiastes 9:5; Psalms 6:5)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   In the Old Testament the dead go to Sheol, for all; different fates only appear in Daniel (c. 165 BC). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheol

17. The idea of eternal hell developed under Persian and Greek influences (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Zoroastrianism (final judgment) and Hellenism (immortal soul, Tartarus); Ehrman, 'Heaven and Hell' (2020). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gehenna

18. Belief in a watching, punishing god increases obedience and cooperation in the group (Leviticus 26:16; Deuteronomy 28:15)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Purzycki et al., Nature 2016; Norenzayan, 'Big Gods' (2013). — https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16980

19. Moralizing gods appeared only after societies became complex (Leviticus 26:16)
   ❔ Not verifiable
   The 2019 study (Whitehouse, Nature) was retracted after critiques; the question remains open. — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03655-4

20. A single person deliberately invented God to control the people (Exodus 20:5)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   It took many generations; control was one function, alongside identity, comfort and explaining disasters. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origins_of_Judaism

21. The traits of the God of the texts mirror the ideals of warrior kings of that age (Exodus 20:5; Deuteronomy 7:2)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Exclusive loyalty, extermination of the enemy and curses also appear in Mesha and Assyrian treaties. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herem_(war_or_property)

22. People tend to attribute their own opinions to God (Exodus 20:5)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Epley et al., PNAS 2009: estimates of 'what God thinks' track the person's own opinion. — https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0908374106

23. The Bible is consistent about punishing children for their parents' sins (Exodus 20:5; Ezekiel 18:20)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Ex 20:5 says yes; Ezek 18:20 says no. They are different voices. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Ezekiel

24. 'God is love' fits, read literally, with the massacre orders (1 John 4:8; Numbers 31:17)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Even apologists and theologians resort to allegory, hyperbole or progressive revelation to reconcile them. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcionism

25. An idea repeated many times seems truer (Deuteronomy 13:6)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Illusory truth effect (Hasher 1977; Fazio et al. 2015). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusory_truth_effect

26. There is a God behind the texts (1 John 4:8)
   ❔ Not verifiable
   Science neither proves nor refutes it. What it shows is that the image of God in the texts was shaped by people. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existence_of_God

grupo: Who created the God of the Bible? The minds behind the text
tema: Conhecimento Solar's opinion: honest verdict on who created the God of the Bible
palavras: was the god of the bible invented
resposta: Verdict: the image of God in the Bible was written by human beings, and that matches reality. Many hands over about a thousand years: tribes with a storm god from the south, kings who needed loyalty, priests in exile who turned defeat into 'punishment for sins', and later teachers who, under Persian and Greek influence, created eternal hell. This God's harshest traits (jealousy, exclusive loyalty, collective punishment, extermination of the enemy) are those of the kings and war gods of the age, as on the Mesha Stele and in Assyrian treaties. A human giving the orders of Numbers 31 or 1 Samuel 15 today would be tried for genocide. And the same book also says 'God is love' and 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father'. They are different human voices that don't agree with each other.
aprofundar:
Where your intuition needs adjusting: it wasn't one person, and control through fear and guilt was a real function, but not the only one. These texts also gave identity, comfort and hope to a small, threatened people. Science neither proves nor refutes that a God exists. What it shows is that the biblical portrait of God bears the marks of those who drew it. Believers were not foolish: they received a story repeated for generations (illusory truth effect — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusory_truth_effect). A calm invitation: read the cited verses in context, check the sources and decide freely, without fear. Sources: Römer — https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674504974 ; Smith — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Early_History_of_God ; Mesha Stele — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesha_Stele ; Rome Statute — https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/RS-Eng.pdf

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Numbers 31:17 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Numbers+31%3A17&version=KJV | 1 Samuel 15:3 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Samuel+15%3A3&version=KJV | 1 John 4:8 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+John+4%3A8&version=KJV | Ezekiel 18:20 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ezekiel+18%3A20&version=KJV
camada3: To contemplate: if the image of God was painted by people, you too can choose which values to keep: mercy, justice, care for others, without needing fear.
